newsitem.title: Russia: Kremlin steps up pressure, threatens Duma.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin steps up pressure, threatens Duma.

text.p: Oleg Sysuyev, a senior reformer in the Russian government, warned parliament on Wednesday that ministers' patience was wearing thin over its resistance to economic change and again raised the threat of new elections.

Sysuyev told a news conference he personally did not favour dissolving the communist-dominated State Duma (lower house) but said the executive could raise the issue "in a tough manner" later this year.
Only President Boris Yeltsin has the right to call an early parliamentary election.

"The Duma is doing all it can to create an extraordinarily tense situation by the autumn, to force the president to change policy. This will not happen," said Sysuyev, a deputy prime minister whose package of bills cutting welfare benefits was rejected by the Duma on Tuesday.

"The situation will be even more difficult in autumn and the question of changing the Duma may be raised by the executive branch. It may raise it in a tough manner," he said, adding that he personally favoured carrying on his "difficult and sometimes repugnant work" with the current chamber.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais on Tuesday accused the Duma of being "incapable of working" after it rose for its summer recess having rejected two of three key pieces of economic reform legislation.
He stressed the question of dissolution was up to Yeltsin.

Asked about Chubais's remarks, Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Wednesday morning: "Despite the Duma's frequent refusal to work with the executive and hide under cover of populism, the executive is inclined to cooperate with the Duma, as it considers this essential for the country."
Asked about the Duma's rejection of the welfare bills on Tuesday, Yastrzhembsky said: "An immediate Kremlin response would be rather improper."

Analysts say regular veiled threats of a dissolution -- more than two years before new parliamentary elections are due in December 1999 -- are designed to discomfit sitting deputies in an attempt to make the Duma more amenable.

Few believe the government, which has already said it will press ahead with reforms without the Duma by using Yeltsin's vast powers to rule by decree, would benefit from elections. Voters are still discontented and would be likely to return an equally uncooperative lower chamber.
